screens.title: The Strategy Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: Today we explore the Strategy pattern, a practical way to make algorithms interchangeable without scattering conditional logic across your code. You will see why a large if–else or switch quickly becomes brittle, and how the Strategy pattern isolates each algorithm behind a shared interface. In real systems you often need to change behavior at runtime — for example calculating shipping costs for different destinations or choosing a payment method — and the Strategy pattern makes that selection explicit, testable, and extensible. We’ll use Java examples from payment processing, document export, and sorting to show how to define a Strategy interface, implement concrete strategies, and let a Context class delegate the work. You will also learn common pitfalls, like carrying state inside strategies or over-engineering simple problems, and practical advice: prefer stateless strategies or let the context own state, design clear interfaces that match the algorithms, and test strategies in isolation. By the end, you’ll know when the pattern clarifies code and when it adds needless complexity.

Second, you will implement the Strategy pattern in Java by defining an interface, writing concrete strategy classes, and creating a context that delegates execution. These skills will help you design code that follows the open/closed principle and is easier to extend and reason about.

screens.title: Why conditionals become a problem
screens.narratorSegment: Begin by recognizing the practical problem the Strategy pattern solves: sprawling conditional logic. When a single class changes its behavior based on many conditions, you often see long if–else chains or switch statements that check types, flags, or configuration. That approach couples the decision logic to implementation details, so adding a new algorithm forces you to edit the same class — violating the open/closed principle. For example, a ShippingCalculator that branches on international, express, or customer loyalty will quickly accumulate special cases and duplicated calculations. The Strategy pattern treats each algorithm as an independent unit: you extract the calculation into its own class that implements a shared interface, and the context simply selects and delegates. A concrete example: instead of a switch that computes shipping by destination codes, define a ShippingCostCalculator interface and multiple implementations like StandardShippingCalculator and InternationalShippingCalculator. A common misconception is that Strategy always requires many classes; in fact, the pattern is worthwhile when behavior varies and will likely change or grow. If there truly is a single stable algorithm, Strategy can be unnecessary boilerplate. Thoughtfully apply Strategy where conditional branching harms extensibility or testability. Reflect: when have you modified a single class to add new behavior and wished you could add a new module instead?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Large conditional blocks hide algorithms and make code brittle; Strategy separates the algorithms into interchangeable classes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Why conditionals
Problem scenario

An e-commerce ShippingCalculator grows conditionals for destination, weight, and loyalty flags. Each new rule modifies the same class, increasing risk of breaking existing calculations.

Common mistake
Put all algorithms in one class behind branches instead of isolating them.
When to avoid
If there is only one algorithm and no expected variation, Strategy may add unnecessary complexity.
Strategy alternative
Extract each calculation into a class implementing ShippingCostCalculator, and let a Context hold and call the chosen strategy. This reduces coupling and makes each algorithm testable alone.
Example card
StandardShippingCalculator
Encapsulates domestic rules. No knowledge of express or international calculations.
Key Takeaway

Replace sprawling conditionals with interchangeable algorithm classes to keep code open for extension and closed for modification.

screens.title: Strategy, Concrete Strategies, Context
screens.narratorSegment: At the heart of Strategy are three roles you will use repeatedly: the Strategy Interface, Concrete Strategies, and the Context. First, the Strategy Interface declares the operation signature that all algorithms share. It defines what the context can call, ensuring interchangeability. Second, Concrete Strategies implement that interface and provide distinct algorithm behaviors — for example, StandardShippingCalculator or ExpressShippingCalculator. Each implementation focuses only on its algorithm, making it easy to test. Third, the Context maintains a reference to a Strategy and delegates calls to it; the Context may offer a setter to change the strategy at runtime. An important design point is where state belongs. The Context should own state that pertains to the overall operation, while strategies should remain stateless or accept any required data via method parameters. A concrete example is a Sorter context that gets a list to sort; you inject a QuickSortStrategy or a MergeSortStrategy and the Context calls sort with the data. A common misconception is thinking the Context must know algorithm details; instead it should only use the common interface. The core benefit is loose coupling: the Context depends on the interface, not on concrete classes.

keyIdea.text: Three roles — interface, implementations, and context — collaborate so algorithms can vary independently from clients.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Components
Strategy Interface
Declares the method signature shared by all algorithms. It must be cohesive and represent the family of algorithms.
Example: ShippingCostCalculator with calculate(Order order).
Concrete Strategies
Implement the interface with specific behavior. Keep them focused and testable in isolation.
Example: ExpressShippingCalculator handles fast delivery rules.
Context
Holds a strategy reference, delegates algorithm calls, and may provide a setter to change strategies at runtime. Owns operation-wide state.
Example: ShippingService calls strategy.calculate(order).
Example
Sorter context + QuickSortStrategy or MergeSortStrategy for different data sizes.
Misconception
Context must implement algorithms — false. Context should only delegate to the strategy interface.
Key Takeaway
Partition responsibilities: interface for contract, strategy for algorithms, context for orchestration.

screens.title: PaymentStrategy example in Java
screens.narratorSegment: Now we walk through the PaymentStrategy example. The interface simply declares a pay operation accepting an amount. Two concrete implementations — a credit card strategy and a PayPal strategy — implement that operation with their behavior. The ShoppingCart context holds a payment strategy reference, accumulates item prices, and delegates the actual payment when checkout is called. This structure demonstrates decoupling: the cart does not know how payment happens, only that the currently set strategy will process the total. A concrete example from the code: the cart adds a laptop and a mouse, then sets a credit card strategy and checks out, producing output that indicates payment by card. Later a different cart sets a PayPal strategy and checks out, producing a different output. A common misconception is that strategies must be singletons; they can be created per use, and if they carry sensitive or mutable data, prefer fresh instances or manage state in the context. Test each strategy independently by calling pay with controlled amounts, and test the context by swapping strategies to confirm delegation works. What would you test first: the concrete strategies in isolation or the context wiring?

keyIdea.title: Concrete code insight
keyIdea.text: The context delegates payment to the injected strategy; changing strategies changes behavior without modifying the cart.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Payment Strategy
Code (excerpt)
<!-- Strategy Interface -->
interface PaymentStrategy {
  void pay(int amount);
}

<!-- Concrete Strategy: Credit Card -->
class CreditCardPayment implements PaymentStrategy {
  private String cardNumber;
  // constructor omitted
  @Override
  public void pay(int amount) {
    System.out.println("Paying " + amount + " using Credit Card: " + cardNumber);
  }
}

<!-- Context: ShoppingCart -->
class ShoppingCart {
  private int totalAmount;
  private PaymentStrategy paymentStrategy;
  public void setPaymentStrategy(PaymentStrategy paymentStrategy) { this.paymentStrategy = paymentStrategy; }
  public void addItem(String item, int price) { this.totalAmount += price; }
  public void checkout() {
    if (paymentStrategy == null) {
      System.out.println("Please select a payment strategy before checking out.");
      return;
    }
    paymentStrategy.pay(totalAmount);
    this.totalAmount = 0;
  }
}
Explanation
  • Interface: single responsibility for payment operation.
  • Concrete strategies: encapsulate payment details and I/O concerns.
  • Context: collects items and delegates payment to the chosen strategy.
Concrete example
Cart sets CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment in separate transactions to show different outputs.
Key Takeaway

Design contexts to accept strategies at runtime so behavior can change without editing the context code.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Document Export
Starter code (template)
// Strategy Interface
interface DocumentExportStrategy {
  void export(String documentContent);
}

// Concrete strategies: PdfExportStrategy, HtmlExportStrategy

// Context: DocumentProcessor
class DocumentProcessor {
  private DocumentExportStrategy exportStrategy;
  public void setExportStrategy(DocumentExportStrategy strategy) { this.exportStrategy = strategy; }
  public void exportDocument(String content) {
    if (exportStrategy == null) {
      System.out.println("No export strategy set. Cannot export document.");
      return;
    }
    exportStrategy.export(content);
  }
}
Notes & example
  • PdfExportStrategy prints a PDF preview line for demo purposes.
  • HtmlExportStrategy wraps content in simple html tags for demonstration.
  • To add PlainTextExportStrategy, implement the same interface and register it with the processor.
Key Takeaway

Use strategy interfaces to add new export formats without modifying the processor code.

screens.title: Strategy vs switch/if-else
screens.narratorSegment: Compare Strategy with a switch or if–else approach to understand trade-offs. A switch statement keeps all logic in one place. This can be simpler for very small problems with no foreseeable change, but it quickly violates the open/closed principle when you add new behaviors. Strategy moves implementations into separate classes, improving extensibility and testability. For example, a DiscountCalculator using a switch requires you to edit the same class whenever you introduce a new customer type. Using Strategy, each discount becomes its own class, and adding a new rule only adds a new strategy. However, Strategy increases the number of classes and can add indirection, which may be unnecessary in trivial cases. A common misconception is assuming Strategy always makes code faster; it usually improves maintainability but not raw performance. Evaluate the expected frequency of change and the need for isolated testing: if both are high, Strategy is a better choice. For a one-off utility with stable behavior, a switch is acceptable. Ask yourself: will I need to add or test new algorithms independently in the future? Strategy vs switch/if-else means use strategy when you expect behavior to vary or need independent testing; prefer simple conditionals for tiny, stable tasks.. In practical terms, trade-offs: extensibility, clarity, and complexity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

If-else / switch

  • Becomes hard to extend and test as cases grow.

Choose Strategy when extensibility and testability outweigh additional classes and indirection.

screens.title: Implementing Strategy in Java
screens.narratorSegment: Follow a practical implementation sequence to ensure the Strategy pattern is applied cleanly. Step one: design the Strategy Interface so that it represents a coherent family of algorithms. Keep parameters and return types consistent across strategies. Step two: implement Concrete Strategies, each focused on a single algorithm. Keep them small and free of unrelated responsibilities. Step three: create the Context that holds a reference to the Strategy and delegates calls. Provide a setter or constructor injection to change strategies. This step-by-step flow reduces coupling, improves clarity, and makes your code easier to extend and maintain. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Implementation
Five steps
  1. Design the Strategy Interface with consistent method signature.
  2. Create Concrete Strategies implementing the interface.
  3. Implement Context that holds and delegates to a Strategy reference.
  4. Wire strategies at runtime through setter or constructor injection.
  5. Unit test strategies and Context behavior independently.
Pitfall & fix
Pitfall: strategies with hidden mutable state. Fix: make strategies stateless or let Context own state and pass it into strategy methods.
Pro-tip
Prefer constructor injection for immutable strategy configuration, and setter injection when runtime swapping is required.
Key Takeaway

Follow a clear sequence from interface to runtime wiring and test each component independently for reliability.

screens.title: Design choices and interface boundaries
screens.narratorSegment: Designing the Strategy Interface correctly is crucial. Start by grouping algorithms that truly belong together — they should accept similar inputs and produce compatible outputs. If two algorithms require very different parameters, they likely do not belong on the same interface. Keep the interface minimal and expressive: avoid exposing context internals directly through the interface. Pass only the data needed for the algorithm as method parameters. Prefer returning results rather than mutating shared objects unless mutation is deliberate and well-documented. Another best practice is to make strategies stateless when possible: stateless implementations are safe to reuse across threads and contexts. If an algorithm requires configuration, accept configuration via constructor parameters or a small configuration object, not via hidden global state. For testing, implement small fixtures that exercise edge cases of each strategy. A common misconception is that larger interfaces are more flexible; in reality, broad interfaces force strategies to implement unrelated concerns and reduce interchangeability. Ask: does every candidate strategy need the same inputs and produce a useful output to the context? Design choices and interface boundaries means make the strategy interface cohesive and minimal so all concrete strategies remain interchangeable and easy to test.. In practical terms, how to define the right strategy interface. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Several mistakes recur when teams adopt Strategy. First, over-engineering: applying Strategy for a single algorithm adds needless classes and indirection. Check whether future variation or independent testing justifies the pattern. Second, hidden or shared mutable state inside strategies creates concurrency bugs when the same strategy instance is reused across contexts. Avoid this by making strategies stateless or by creating fresh instances per use, and keep mutable state in the Context. Third, poorly defined interfaces that try to serve incompatible algorithms force strategies to implement unused parameters or to rely on context internals. If algorithms require different inputs, split them into different family interfaces. Fourth, mixing responsibilities: strategies should only implement the algorithm; they should not perform unrelated tasks like logging or UI changes. Centralize cross-cutting concerns elsewhere. To avoid these pitfalls, review each strategy for single responsibility, keep state explicit, and prefer composition over inheritance when sharing utilities. A quick check: if adding a new algorithm requires editing multiple classes, the design likely needs improvement. screens.title: Switching strategies at runtime
screens.narratorSegment: One of Strategy’s most useful features is runtime swapping of algorithms. There are several common mechanisms to choose and inject strategies: explicit setter calls from client code, configuration-based wiring at startup, or dependency injection frameworks. For interactive scenarios, like a user choosing a payment method, the context can set the chosen strategy just before performing an operation. For configuration-driven scenarios, the application can read settings at startup and instantiate the appropriate strategy. The important design detail is ensuring the Context offers a clear, documented way to change strategies and that any required configuration is provided when the strategy is created. Also consider lifecycle: if a strategy holds resources, make sure you manage creation and disposal appropriately. A clear example is a Sorter that selects a QuickSortStrategy for large arrays and a BubbleSortStrategy for small arrays based on data size before sorting. A common misconception is that swapping strategies is expensive; creating lightweight strategy instances or using pooling keeps overhead low while preserving modularity. How will you choose strategies in your next design: user choice, config, or automatic heuristics? Switching strategies at runtime means select strategies at runtime via setters, configuration, or dependency injection so behavior adapts without code changes.. In practical terms, configuration, user choice, and dependency injection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Testing and safety considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Safety and correctness are essential when swapping algorithms. Each concrete strategy must validate its inputs because assumptions can vary across algorithms. For example, a financial payment strategy must validate amounts and card fields, while an export strategy must handle empty or malformed content gracefully. Testing should include unit tests for each concrete strategy that exercise normal, boundary, and error conditions. Additionally, integration tests should verify the Context delegates correctly and that switching strategies produces the expected end-to-end behavior. Performance is another concern: different algorithms can have widely different costs. Profile representative scenarios and choose the appropriate strategy when runtime selection depends on performance. A misconception is assuming tests for the Context are sufficient; instead, test both strategies and the Context wiring. For strategies that touch external systems, use mocks in tests to simulate external behavior. Finally, in security-sensitive domains, treat strategy selection as a trusted decision and restrict which strategies can be used in production. Testing and safety considerations means validate inputs inside strategies, test each strategy independently, and profile when performance matters.. screens.title: When to choose Strategy in system design
screens.narratorSegment: Use Strategy in system design when you see certain signals in your codebase. First, frequent edits to a single method to add new cases suggest the open/closed principle is being violated. Second, if individual behaviors need isolated tests or different deployment schedules, Strategy allows you to test and evolve algorithms independently. Third, when runtime selection is a business requirement — for example, selecting a shipping or payment method based on user choice or configuration — Strategy models that requirement directly. Fourth, when you want to reuse algorithms across different contexts, encapsulation makes reuse straightforward. Conversely, avoid Strategy for tiny utilities with no prospect of change or where the indirection would harm readability for future maintainers. A practical example: a logging subsystem that can write to files, a database, or a remote server is a great candidate for Strategy because destinations are interchangeable and require separate implementations. Before refactoring, list the behaviors, their inputs, and how often they change, then decide whether extracting strategies reduces future risk more than it increases class count. When to choose Strategy in system design means choose strategy when behaviors vary, need independent testing, or must be selected at runtime; avoid it for one-off stable logic.. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s summarize the essential ideas. First, the Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable so the algorithm can vary independently from clients. Second, the Strategy Interface is the contract all concrete algorithms implement; it must be cohesive and consistent across strategies. Third, Concrete Strategies provide the actual algorithm implementations, focused on a single concern and easy to test. Fourth, the Context holds a reference to a strategy and delegates execution; it should own shared state while strategies remain stateless or accept necessary data via parameters. Fifth, avoid overuse: prefer Strategy when behaviors vary, need independent tests, or require runtime selection. Finally, validate inputs, manage resource lifecycle, and profile performance where necessary. These concepts together help you design systems that are open for extension and closed for modification.

fullNarratorScript:
Today we explore the Strategy pattern, a practical way to make algorithms interchangeable without scattering conditional logic across your code. You will see why a large if–else or switch quickly becomes brittle, and how the Strategy pattern isolates each algorithm behind a shared interface. In real systems you often need to change behavior at runtime — for example calculating shipping costs for different destinations or choosing a payment method — and the Strategy pattern makes that selection explicit, testable, and extensible. We’ll use Java examples from payment processing, document export, and sorting to show how to define a Strategy interface, implement concrete strategies, and let a Context class delegate the work. You will also learn common pitfalls, like carrying state inside strategies or over-engineering simple problems, and practical advice: prefer stateless strategies or let the context own state, design clear interfaces that match the algorithms, and test strategies in isolation. By the end, you’ll know when the pattern clarifies code and when it adds needless complexity.

By the end of this chapter you will have four concrete skills. First, you will understand the intent and core principles of the Strategy pattern: how it separates algorithm selection from algorithm implementation so a client can change behavior without modifying internal logic. For example, you will be able to explain how a shipping service swaps calculators based on destination or customer type. Second, you will implement the Strategy pattern in Java by defining an interface, writing concrete strategy classes, and creating a context that delegates execution. You will practice with the payment processor example and the document export template. Third, you will analyze situations where Strategy improves flexibility and maintainability, identifying candidates like discount calculation or logging destinations, and contrasting them with cases where conditional logic is simpler. Fourth, you will recognize common pitfalls and best practices: prefer stateless strategies, keep interfaces cohesive, validate inputs in each strategy, and test strategies in isolation. These skills will help you design code that follows the open/closed principle and is easier to extend and reason about.

This second objectives slide emphasizes applied skills and assessment readiness. You will implement the payment strategy example in Java: define a PaymentStrategy interface and at least two concrete strategies, then create a ShoppingCart context that accepts a strategy and delegates payment processing. Practically, you will run the example to observe different outputs for credit card and PayPal payments. Next, you will complete a hands-on activity: add export strategies for a document processor and demonstrate switching at runtime. That exercise teaches interface design and how to keep algorithms isolated. Finally, you will learn to evaluate when Strategy is the right fit by comparing it to a simple switch-based approach. You will write a short design note describing which approach you chose and why, covering trade-offs like testability, extensibility, and complexity. These tasks build confidence: you won’t only read patterns, you will implement, run, and explain them.

Begin by recognizing the practical problem the Strategy pattern solves: sprawling conditional logic. When a single class changes its behavior based on many conditions, you often see long if–else chains or switch statements that check types, flags, or configuration. That approach couples the decision logic to implementation details, so adding a new algorithm forces you to edit the same class — violating the open/closed principle. For example, a ShippingCalculator that branches on international, express, or customer loyalty will quickly accumulate special cases and duplicated calculations. The Strategy pattern treats each algorithm as an independent unit: you extract the calculation into its own class that implements a shared interface, and the context simply selects and delegates. A concrete example: instead of a switch that computes shipping by destination codes, define a ShippingCostCalculator interface and multiple implementations like StandardShippingCalculator and InternationalShippingCalculator. A common misconception is that Strategy always requires many classes; in fact, the pattern is worthwhile when behavior varies and will likely change or grow. If there truly is a single stable algorithm, Strategy can be unnecessary boilerplate. Thoughtfully apply Strategy where conditional branching harms extensibility or testability. Reflect: when have you modified a single class to add new behavior and wished you could add a new module instead?

At the heart of Strategy are three roles you will use repeatedly: the Strategy Interface, Concrete Strategies, and the Context. First, the Strategy Interface declares the operation signature that all algorithms share. It defines what the context can call, ensuring interchangeability. Second, Concrete Strategies implement that interface and provide distinct algorithm behaviors — for example, StandardShippingCalculator or ExpressShippingCalculator. Each implementation focuses only on its algorithm, making it easy to test. Third, the Context maintains a reference to a Strategy and delegates calls to it; the Context may offer a setter to change the strategy at runtime. An important design point is where state belongs. The Context should own state that pertains to the overall operation, while strategies should remain stateless or accept any required data via method parameters. A concrete example is a Sorter context that gets a list to sort; you inject a QuickSortStrategy or a MergeSortStrategy and the Context calls sort with the data. A common misconception is thinking the Context must know algorithm details; instead it should only use the common interface. The core benefit is loose coupling: the Context depends on the interface, not on concrete classes.

Now we walk through the PaymentStrategy example. The interface simply declares a pay operation accepting an amount. Two concrete implementations — a credit card strategy and a PayPal strategy — implement that operation with their behavior. The ShoppingCart context holds a payment strategy reference, accumulates item prices, and delegates the actual payment when checkout is called. This structure demonstrates decoupling: the cart does not know how payment happens, only that the currently set strategy will process the total. A concrete example from the code: the cart adds a laptop and a mouse, then sets a credit card strategy and checks out, producing output that indicates payment by card. Later a different cart sets a PayPal strategy and checks out, producing a different output. A common misconception is that strategies must be singletons; they can be created per use, and if they carry sensitive or mutable data, prefer fresh instances or manage state in the context. Test each strategy independently by calling pay with controlled amounts, and test the context by swapping strategies to confirm delegation works. What would you test first: the concrete strategies in isolation or the context wiring?

This screen walks through the hands-on document export activity. The Strategy Interface is DocumentExportStrategy with an export method accepting document content. Two concrete strategies, PdfExportStrategy and HtmlExportStrategy, implement export with their respective formatting. The DocumentProcessor context holds a reference to the export strategy and delegates exportDocument calls. When you change the strategy at runtime, the same document content is formatted differently without altering the processor code. A concrete code template prints a short preview to illustrate the behavior. Common mistakes include having strategies assume external state like file paths; instead pass required data into the export method or let the context supply it. Another issue is duplicating trimming or preview code across strategies — factor shared utility into a helper class. For testing, run export strategies individually with sample content to verify output formatting, then test the processor by swapping strategies and asserting the processor delegates correctly. Think about how you would add a PlainTextExportStrategy and what parts of the interface must remain stable. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Compare Strategy with a switch or if–else approach to understand trade-offs. A switch statement keeps all logic in one place. This can be simpler for very small problems with no foreseeable change, but it quickly violates the open/closed principle when you add new behaviors. Strategy moves implementations into separate classes, improving extensibility and testability. For example, a DiscountCalculator using a switch requires you to edit the same class whenever you introduce a new customer type. Using Strategy, each discount becomes its own class, and adding a new rule only adds a new strategy. However, Strategy increases the number of classes and can add indirection, which may be unnecessary in trivial cases. A common misconception is assuming Strategy always makes code faster; it usually improves maintainability but not raw performance. Evaluate the expected frequency of change and the need for isolated testing: if both are high, Strategy is a better choice. For a one-off utility with stable behavior, a switch is acceptable. Ask yourself: will I need to add or test new algorithms independently in the future? Strategy vs switch/if-else means use strategy when you expect behavior to vary or need independent testing; prefer simple conditionals for tiny, stable tasks.. In practical terms, trade-offs: extensibility, clarity, and complexity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Step three: create the Context that holds a reference to the Strategy and delegates calls. Provide a setter or constructor injection to change strategies. Step four: wire together at runtime, for example selecting a strategy based on configuration, user choice, or runtime data, and then call the delegated method. Step five: test. Write unit tests for each concrete strategy, verifying behavior with representative inputs. Also write tests for the Context to confirm it delegates correctly when different strategies are injected. A common misconception is to let strategies share mutable state; instead, pass data explicitly or let the Context manage state. This step-by-step flow reduces coupling, improves clarity, and makes your code easier to extend and maintain. One of Strategy’s most useful features is runtime swapping of algorithms. There are several common mechanisms to choose and inject strategies: explicit setter calls from client code, configuration-based wiring at startup, or dependency injection frameworks. For configuration-driven scenarios, the application can read settings at startup and instantiate the appropriate strategy. Safety and correctness are essential when swapping algorithms. Each concrete strategy must validate its inputs because assumptions can vary across algorithms. For example, a financial payment strategy must validate amounts and card fields, while an export strategy must handle empty or malformed content gracefully. Use Strategy in system design when you see certain signals in your codebase. First, frequent edits to a single method to add new cases suggest the open/closed principle is being violated. Second, if individual behaviors need isolated tests or different deployment schedules, Strategy allows you to test and evolve algorithms independently. Third, when runtime selection is a business requirement — for example, selecting a shipping or payment method based on user choice or configuration — Strategy models that requirement directly. Fourth, when you want to reuse algorithms across different contexts, encapsulation makes reuse straightforward. Conversely, avoid Strategy for tiny utilities with no prospect of change or where the indirection would harm readability for future maintainers. A practical example: a logging subsystem that can write to files, a database, or a remote server is a great candidate for Strategy because destinations are interchangeable and require separate implementations. Before refactoring, list the behaviors, their inputs, and how often they change, then decide whether extracting strategies reduces future risk more than it increases class count. Let’s summarize the essential ideas. First, the Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable so the algorithm can vary independently from clients. Second, the Strategy Interface is the contract all concrete algorithms implement; it must be cohesive and consistent across strategies. Third, Concrete Strategies provide the actual algorithm implementations, focused on a single concern and easy to test. Fourth, the Context holds a reference to a strategy and delegates execution; it should own shared state while strategies remain stateless or accept necessary data via parameters. Fifth, avoid overuse: prefer Strategy when behaviors vary, need independent tests, or require runtime selection. Finally, validate inputs, manage resource lifecycle, and profile performance where necessary. These concepts together help you design systems that are open for extension and closed for modification.

A final quick reference to help you apply Strategy in everyday design. First card: Loose coupling — the Context depends on an interface, not concrete implementations, so algorithms can change independently. Second card: Stateless strategies — keep algorithm state out of shared instances; pass necessary data or configure during construction so concurrency issues are avoided. Third card: When not to use Strategy — do not apply it when behavior is stable and unlikely to change, because it adds class count and indirection. Keep these three ideas in mind as design checks when you refactor conditional logic into strategies.
